jurors.reason: The record gives me no base rate to lean on, and on its own numbers the plan stakes a job and all the savings on a more-than-fourfold jump in sales extrapolated from one 40-sale, three-month total with no trend and no stopping point.
jurors.fact: Covering the $1,600 rent from gross sales alone takes about 57 sales a month at $28, over four times the roughly 13 a month in the record's only data point (40 sales in 3 months).
jurors.flip: The case included a month-by-month sales record showing sales rising fast enough to reach about 57 a month inside the five months the savings cover.

jurors.reason: I wouldn't let anyone I love quit nursing and stake the $8,000 they have saved on candles that gross about $373 a month against $1,600 rent, with no stop point and no word on whether they could go back.
jurors.fact: 40 sales at $28 over three months is about $373 a month, which the defense concedes covers under a quarter of the $1,600 rent, so at today's pace the $8,000 saved is gone in under seven months even if every dollar of sales were profit and rent were the only bill.
jurors.flip: the record showed a firm way back to nursing work, such as an approved leave or a promised re-hire, so that failing would cost the savings but not the nursing income for good.

jurors.reason: As the lawyer, I see a plan that gives up the paycheck before papering anything: candles made at home carry fire, burn and lease exposure, and the record shows no liability insurance, lease permission, tax plan, health coverage or license upkeep behind them, only an $8,000 cushion that is five months of rent.
jurors.fact: "They make the candles at home" and rent is $1,600 a month, so a wax-and-flame business sits in what is presumably a leased home, yet the record is silent on the lease, any insurance and which country's rules apply.
jurors.flip: The case showed the home business already papered: the landlord's written consent to run it from the home and an insurance policy covering product liability for it.
